StateScribe employs a dual-layer memory architecture that inte-
grates episodic scene memory and object-centric temporal memory
to enable scalable and structured change tracking. It provides both
live descriptions of the current scene, and descriptions of what has
changed, when and where it occurred across revisits, such as “The
shop on your right has a “CLOSED” sign; it was open at this time
last week.” Our evaluation shows that StateScribe maintains high
accuracy (𝐹1-score = 83.1%) across 11 revisits, while remaining low-
latency (mean<1.42s) and memory-efficient (<55MB) across 110
revisits. A user study with nine BLV participants demonstrates that
StateScribe improves change awareness across revisits in three
real-world locations. Finally, we discuss implications for long-term
AI-assisted companions that support broader change observation
using multimodal sensing, extend beyond changes to other memory
capabilities, and adapt to individual users, intents, and contexts.
1
Introduction
Real-world environments evolve continuously with many unantic-
ipated changes, yet blind and low-vision (BLV) individuals often
have limited access to information that helps them understand how
familiar spaces transform over time. For example, newly introduced
obstacles, relocated objects in shared spaces, content changes (e.g.,
price updates), or layout modifications can pose safety risks and
increase cognitive burden. Despite these challenges, there remains
a limited understanding of what constitutes meaningful real-world
changes for BLV individuals, and how to convey them effectively.
While existing human-powered services (e.g., Be My Eyes [3],
Aira [2]), AI-powered visual assistive technologies (e.g., Seeing
AI [5] Be My AI [1], WorldScribe [11]), or live video AI (e.g., Chat-
GPT Live Video [6], Gemini Live [4]) can describe immediate sur-
roundings, they typically operate as one-off sessions that retain
only within-session memory. As a result, they lack persistent 3D
spatial memory of a location [13] and mechanisms for surfacing
meaningful changes across revisits. Enabling such longitudinal as-
sistance poses several challenges: (i) Maintaining longitudinal
memory in 3D space is difficult, as systems must identify and
store the most relevant observations from the 3D real world with-
out overloading with redundant information. (ii) Scaling memory
storage and retrieval over extended use is difficult, as spatial
and temporal data grow continuously, increasing retrieval latency
and confusion. (iii) Incorporating change-awareness into real-
time interactions can easily overwhelm users, especially if
updates are frequent and noisy.
Based on a survey of 33 BLV individuals, we identified categories
of changes that are difficult to perceive yet significantly affect daily
life, such as newly introduced obstacles (e.g., scattered packages in
shared apartments), changes to signage along routine commuting
routes (e.g., removed or added signage), and updated pricing or
layout during grocery shopping. To address these challenges, we
present StateScribe, a system designed to support accessible aware-
ness of real-world changes by using a smartphone interface and
sensor data. StateScribe employs a dual-layer memory architecture
that integrates Episodic Scene Memory (ESM) and Object-centric
Temporal Memory (OTM). Specifically, ESM continuously updates
information from recent visits within a bounded context window,
archiving older data to maintain an up-to-date representation of the
scene over time. In contrast, OTM selectively maintains key objects,
tracking their states and spatial locations across visits while record-
ing meaningful changes. This design enables scalable, structured,
and efficient storage and retrieval.
Using these memory structures and smartphone 3D data (e.g.,
RGB-D images and camera intrinsics), StateScribe retrieves ESM
and OTM by querying the current camera pose to identify the most
recent frames from prior visits and detect significant changes. Based
on 3D data and spatial correspondences, it generates descriptions
that clearly communicate what has changed, and when and
where the change occurred. For example, a user revisiting the
market (Figure 1b) a week later might hear: “The fruit stand at your
10 o’clock is selling watermelon and guava; it sold apples and oranges
last week,” “The bakery on your right now shows a ‘CLOSED’ sign; it
was open at this time last week,” or “A construction site is at your 1
o’clock, 10 feet away.” Beyond change descriptions, StateScribe also
provides live descriptions (Figure 1a) to support real-time scene
understanding. StateScribe also enables interactive exploration of
how their environment has evolved, where users can query via
speech, e.g., “Has it blossomed now?”, with responses: “Yes, the trees
have blossomed; they had not last week”(Figure 1b).
In a technical evaluation against two baselines, a Live model that
actively prompts for change detection and a Offline video model
that processes full-visit videos, StateScribe achieved an 𝐹1-score
of 83.1% across 11 visits (291 changes), outperforming the Live
model (40.1%) and Offline video model (27.4%). It also showed higher
spatial accuracy, with lower clock-direction errors (in hour units;
M=0.24 vs. 1.98 and 1.86) and smaller distance estimation errors (in
feet; M=0.68 vs. 5.29 and 6.49). Additionally, StateScribe remained
low-latency (mean<1.42s) and memory-efficient (<55MB) across
110 revisits to simulate long-term use. A user study with nine
BLV participants demonstrated that StateScribe enhanced change
awareness across revisits in three real-world locations (e.g., office,
grocery store, outdoor courtyard). Finally, we discuss implications
for long-term AI-assisted companions that support broader change
observation using multimodal sensing, extend beyond changes to
other memory capabilities, and adapt to individual users, intents,
and contexts.
2
Related Work
StateScribe builds on prior work to provide BLV people with vi-
sual descriptions for real-world understanding, as well as traditional
and AI-enabled memory-augmented systems. In what follows, we
describe our motivation from prior related work and research gaps.
2.1
Describing Visual Information for BLV
People
Textual descriptions are essential for making digital and physical
information accessible to BLV people. Recent advances in VLMs en-
abled automated image descriptions and conversational interaction,
reducing reliance on human-authored alt text. These capabilities
allowed BLV users to quickly obtain visual summaries and interac-
tively explore details, which are increasingly integrated into social
network platforms (e.g., Facebook [61]) and assistive apps (e.g., See-
ing AI [5], Be My AI [1]). In addition, prior work has explored

Beyond visual descriptions, prior work in computer vision devel-
oped models for detecting and summarizing visual changes across
images [21, 33]. In parallel, HCI researchers explored systems that
describe visual differences between image pairs to support an ac-
cessible collaborative slide editing [49], image editing [12, 32, 64],
and graphics and 3D geometry editing [65, 66]. However, support
for detecting and describing real-world visual changes remains lim-
ited. Environments change continuously and unpredictably, which
can impact BLV individuals’ daily lives. For instance, unexpected
barriers in outdoor environments [17, 18, 60], relocated objects
in indoor shared spaces [48, 57], or seasonal product rearrange-
ments and price updates in retail environments [35, 40, 56, 63]
could potentially introduce safety risks and cognitive burdens for
BLV individuals. To close these gaps, we first categorized meaning-
ful changes through a formative study and developed StateScribe,
a system that possesses spatial and temporal memory to detect
and describe meaningful changes across visits on familiar routes or
locations, beyond live descriptions of immediate surroundings.
2.2
Human Memory-Augmented Interactions
Early work in human memory-augmented interactions [37] took
the form of lifelogging systems, enabling applications such as so-
cial or audio reminders [26], contextual suggestions [51], sharing
everyday moments [26], and support for people with memory im-
pairments [29, 41, 42]. While effective, these systems faced key
challenges related to capturing meaningful data, managing storage
constraints, and enabling timely retrieval of past data.
First, they typically relied on continuously capturing large por-
tions of everyday experiences across modalities, including pho-
tos [22, 23, 29, 47], videos [30, 46, 53], audio signals [26, 51, 59, 69],
GPS data [22, 23, 30, 51], and physiological signals [8–10, 27, 30, 34].
However, such continuous recording imposed substantial storage
demands, limiting long-term usability. To mitigate this, some sys-
tems adopted selective capture strategies, such as manual record-
ing [37], biosignal-based triggers (e.g., startle responses [27] or emo-
tional changes [34]), and spatial triggers [23] (e.g., remaining within
a 50-meter radius for over five minutes). Beyond storage, accessing
and making use of captured data remained challenging. Traditional
interfaces are primarily supported browsing by time [16], loca-
tion [55], or both [15, 22, 23], offering limited support for efficient
navigation and retrieval of relevant past information.
Recent advances in multi-modal large language models (MLLMs)
and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) have improved how
memory is captured, stored, and retrieved. Prior computer vision
work explored memory structures for embodied agents across tasks
such as spatial reasoning [68], robot navigation [31], and persis-
tent 3D scene understanding [20], but these were optimized for
offline accuracy rather than real-time human-AI interaction. In
contrast, systems like Memoro [69] store conversational snippets
as lightweight memory units for efficient live retrieval, while Om-
niQuery [43] extracts semantic signals from images and videos for
structured indexing. Memory Reviver further organizes photo col-
lections into hierarchical representations to support conversational
retrieval for BLV users [62]. However, these largely text-based ap-
proaches remain limited in dynamic real-world settings, where rich
visual information cannot be fully captured through text alone.
To address this, StateScribe employs a novel memory architec-
ture that captures visual information from camera frames and selec-
tively retains meaningful object changes in both visual and textual
modalities across recent visits, while archiving outdated data to
maintain lightweight storage for extended use. StateScribe also
has an efficient memory storage and retrieval pipeline that lever-
ages camera poses and visual analysis, enabling it to proactively
announce changes in real-time and across visits.
3
Formative Study: Understanding Real-World
Changes Meaningful to BLV People
To address a key question, What constitutes meaningful real-world
changes for BLV people?, we conducted a survey (Appendix 8) with
33 BLV people (10 male, 21 female, 2 non-binary; mean age=45.1,
SD=15.9), including 16 blind and 17 low-vision individuals (Table 1).
3.1
Results
Reported below are our findings on common real-world changes
and their impact on the everyday life of these BLV individuals.
3.1.1
Changes during daily commutes. Participants frequently re-
ported temporary barriers near construction sites (N=28), such
as fences, traffic cones, scaffolding, tape, and detours, which ob-
structed their usual routes. The construction sites also sometimes
removed or obscured key landmarks (N=7), including signage,
pedestrian signals, and tactile paving. In addition, natural changes,
such as snowbanks, flooding (N=23), and fallen or overhanging
tree branches, further disrupted familiar routes. Furthermore, the
replacement of familiar landmarks caused confusion, as F15
noted: “A bus stop that used to be just a bench was replaced with
a metal shelter. I didn’t expect it and bumped into it.” While some
high-level changes can be anticipated (e.g., via weather or transit
updates), pedestrian-level changes remained difficult to detect, with
little warning (F20: “no commotion or construction noise”). Partici-
pants often noticed them only after collisions, cane detection, or
others’ alerts.
3.1.2
Changes during grocery shopping. Beyond temporary bar-
riers (e.g., carts or displays blocking aisles), participants reported
spatial changes during grocery shopping, including product relo-
cations (N=24) and aisle rearrangements (N=21). These unexpected
changes caused frustration (F18: “The chip aisle became canned food
that I had to find someone to locate it.”). Also, price changes and
sales signage (N=19) often went unnoticed, leading to surprise
at checkout (F6: “I defaulted to the old price.”). To cope with these
changes, some participants used human assistance (e.g., Aira [2])
or AI-powered apps (e.g., Seeing AI [5]), occasionally scanning the
environment to locate items (F28). However, most relied on nearby
shoppers or store staff and expressed a desire for advance awareness
of such changes.

Changes within the home. Participants frequently encoun-

3.2
Summary of Meaningful Visual Changes
In sum, participants mainly relied on memory or direct encoun-
ters to navigate familiar environments, occasionally using assistive
tools (e.g., white canes, mobile AT) to manage unexpected changes.
However, awareness remained largely reactive, highlighting the
need for proactive information and advance alerts to reduce navi-
gation difficulties, hazards, and frustration. Based on these insights,
we categorize meaningful changes as follows:
(i) Object-Level Changes: Changes involving the presence or the
identity of individual objects at a location.
– Appeared: Newly introduced objects not previously present
(e.g., construction barriers, clutter).
– Removed: Previously existing objects that are no longer
present (e.g., missing landmarks or signage).
– Replaced: Objects substituted by different ones at the same
location (e.g., a bench replaced by a bus shelter).
(ii) Spatial Changes: Changes that alter the arrangement or navi-
gability of the environment.
– Relocated: Objects moved to new locations (e.g., product
relocations in stores).
– Layout Changes: Modifications to spatial layout that affect
navigation (e.g., aisle rearrangements, blocked pathways).
(iii) Attribute Changes: Changes in the properties or state of exist-
ing objects without altering their identity or position (e.g., price
changes, signage updates, on/off status).
4
StateScribe
StateScribe is a system with spatial and temporal memory that ob-
serves and describes real-world changes across visits, going beyond
live descriptions of the current scene.
For example, when a BLV user explores a new market (Figure 1),
StateScribe provides live descriptions for scene understanding, such
as “I see a fruit stand with apples and oranges” or “I see a bakery with
an ‘OPEN’ sign on its door.” Meanwhile, it continuously builds a
memory from captured frames. Upon revisiting the market a week
later, StateScribe compares the current view with stored memory
and announces changes during navigation, e.g., “The fruit stand at
your 10 o’clock is selling watermelon and guava; it sold apples and
oranges last week,” “The bakery on your right now shows a ‘CLOSED’
sign; it was open at this time last week,” or “A construction site is at
your 1 o’clock, 10 feet away.” Users can also query temporal changes
via speech, e.g., “Has it blossomed now?”, receiving responses such
as “Yes, the trees have blossomed; they had not last week.” Below, we
describe how StateScribe achieves this experience with different
system modules.
4.1
Memory Construction Module
In this module, StateScribe streams essential sensor data from the
smartphone to the backend for processing and storage within a
novel dual-layer memory architecture: (i) an Episodic Scene Mem-
ory and (ii) an Object-Centric Temporal Memory. These memory
structures are informed by our formative study, which shows that
observed changes primarily fall into three categories: single-object
changes, spatial changes (e.g., multi-object rearrangement), and
attribute changes within an object. However, this design may be
limited in capturing fast motion or activity-based changes, which

Episodic Scene Memory (ESM). To capture the user’s visual
context in real time, we design ESM to retain full observations
within a configurable temporal context window (e.g., the last 10
days, 5 hours, or single visit), while archiving older data (Figure 2a).
ESM serves as the primary memory retrieval source, storing data
streamed from the mobile app to the backend at one data frame per
second (FPS), including RGB-D frames, confidence maps, camera
poses, and associated metadata. Upon receipt, the backend resizes
images, refines depth using confidence maps, generates visual em-
beddings, and asynchronously compresses and stores each instance
as a scene object on local disk.
Object-centric Temporal Memory (OTM). To enable persis-
tent tracking of key objects, we introduce OTM, an object-centric
memory layer that maintains long-term object dynamics beyond
ESM’s temporal window. Specifically, OTM maintains a collection
of tracked real-world objects, each represented as a chronological
sequence of discrete snapshots. Each snapshot captures the object’s
state at a specific moment, including its status relative to the previ-
ous scene (e.g., appeared, disappeared, replaced), description, visual
embedding, and a world-anchored 3D bounding box (Figure 3f,g).
A new OTM entry is created when a change is detected for an
object (e.g., it appears, disappears, or is replaced). A new snapshot
is appended to an existing entry when a changed object shares a
similar 3D location with a prior OTM object, which we detail next.
4.2
Change Detection and Memory Update
Module
In this module, StateScribe identifies changes when a user revisits
a location by comparing the current frame with its ESM and OTM
constructed from prior visits. The process involves: (i) selecting a
reference frame from ESM, (ii) comparing reference and current
frames to detect changes, and (iii) updating OTM. We develop
algorithms and integrate lightweight VLMs to balance accuracy
and latency for live interactions (Section 4.7).

4.3
Live Description Generation Module
In this module, StateScribe generates live visual descriptions to
support the scene understanding. Unlike prior systems that use
multiple VLMs and adaptive prompting for context-aware descrip-
tions [11, 14], StateScribe adopts a simplified approach using frame
filtering and a single VLM with a fixed prompt (Prompt# 2). To de-
tect new scenes, it computes visual embeddings for incoming frames
and compares them with the most recently described frame using
cosine similarity; frames exceeding a threshold (𝜏visual) are treated
as redundant and skipped. To further reduce repetition, generated
descriptions are also compared via text embeddings with prior
outputs, and those exceeding a threshold (𝜏text) are discarded. The
remaining descriptions are queued for presentation (Section 4.5).
We empirically set 𝜏visual = 0.85 and 𝜏text = 0.80 by default.
4.4
Interactive Q&A Module
In this module, StateScribe allows users to interrupt ongoing de-
scriptions and issue queries. It supports change-related queries over
single or multiple objects across time, within specified intervals,
and their spatial variations. This is achieved by a Q&A agent that
interprets each query and invokes tools over ESM, OTM, and spa-
tial data (Prompt# 4): (i) ESM retrieval for current scene queries,
returning the 𝑁most recent frames; (ii) OTM retrieval for temporal
changes, returning recent object snapshots with distance and di-
rection; and (iii) Spatial information retrieval for spatial queries,
returning object locations (e.g., “11 o’clock, 5 feet away”). These
tools are composed based on query intent. For example, “Where
is the cone?” uses ESM retrieval and Spatial information retrieval,
while “What changed since my last visit?” uses OTM retrieval.
4.5
Description Scheduling & Delivery Module
In this module, StateScribe coordinates change snapshots, live de-
scriptions, and interactive Q&A. Visual queries are prioritized, after
which live and change descriptions resume. StateScribe maintains a
buffer (𝑁= 3) of recent live descriptions and change snapshots. Live
descriptions that persist beyond a time threshold (e.g., 6 seconds)
are considered outdated and discarded, while change snapshots
(e.g., appeared, removed, content changed), along with their images
and 3D locations, are retained. Using this aggregated context in a
single prompt (# 3), StateScribe employs a VLM to infer higher-level
events, such as object replacement (via overlapping 3D positions) or
movement (via disappearance and reappearance across locations).
4.6
Mobile User Interface
StateScribe provides a mobile app interface (Figure 2a). The home
screen displays visits as cards, each with a thumbnail and an AI-
generated title. When returning to a location, users can select the
corresponding card to open a live camera view for relocalization and
resume StateScribe’s memory for that place. For new locations, they
can create a visit using the “Add” button. Users can also rename or
delete visits. While the current interface requires users to manually
recall and select past visits, future iterations could incorporate GPS
or indoor localization data to automatically cluster visits or create
a new visit upon arrival at a new location.

5
Technical Evaluation
We conducted a technical evaluation to assess whether StateScribe
(i) captures and preserves longitudinal memory across repeated
visits, (ii) scales efficiently as stored data grows over extended use,
and (iii) improves real-time awareness of changes in 3D physical
environments during interactive use.
5.1
Datasets
To simulate extended use, we constructed a dataset of repeated visits
to the same environments over time. The dataset includes three
environments (Figure 7): (i) a shared office with varying objects
on tables, (ii) a grocery store with densely arranged items across
shelves, and (iii) an outdoor courtyard featuring signs and barriers.
Each scenario contains 11 recorded visits (around 2–4 minutes per
visit), including a video, RGB-D frames, camera intrinsics, and poses,
capturing observations at different time points. We systematically
introduced object changes based on the spatial layout of the shared
office, 104 for the grocery, and 83 for the outdoor scenario. In
total, the dataset contains 291 annotated changes, labeled by three
researchers with 3D world locations, object identities, and change
categories.
5.2
Baseline Conditions and Evaluation Metrics
To evaluate the effectiveness of StateScribe’s design, we compared
it against two VLM-only baselines: a Live model and a Offline video
model. For both baselines, we concatenated the recorded videos
from multiple visits in the same scenario and sampled them at 1 FPS.
In the Live model, we prompted the VLM (i.e., gemini-3-flash- pre-
view) at 1 FPS to approximate real-time interaction similar to State-
Scribe (Prompt# 6). This baseline examines whether StateScribe
improves over a direct VLM-only real-time pipeline. In the Offline
video model condition, we provided the concatenated 1 FPS video
to gemini-3.1-pro as a single input for detecting changes within or
across visits (Prompt# 5). This baseline evaluates StateScribe against
an offline setting that processes all observations jointly rather than
sequentially. In this baseline comparison evaluation, we used the
same Gemini model family as in StateScribe to isolate the effect of
system design rather than differences across model families.
We adopted an LLM-as-judge approach using Gemini 3.1 Pro to
evaluate predictions, including object, location, change type, and
descriptions (e.g., “The white Milano cookie box has been removed
from the shelf.”), against ground truth. We reported overall perfor-
mance using 𝐹1-score, recall, and precision. We further analyzed the
raw number of outputs to assess repetitiveness and coverage, and
then evaluated spatial accuracy, including clock and distance errors,
under each condition. We repeated the same evaluation on data
collected from BLV participants in our user study. Finally, to assess
scalability, we simulated extended use by concatenating 11 visits
10 times (110 visits in total), to measure storage and latency.
5.3

User Study
Next, we conducted a user study with 9 BLV participants to under-
stand: (i) How effectively does StateScribe support users in perceiv-
ing and understanding changes in different environments? (ii) How
do participants perceive the user experience of StateScribe?
6.1
Participants
We recruited 9 BLV participants (6 Male and 3 Female) using email
lists for local accessibility organizations, prior contacts, and snow-
ball sampling (Table 2). Participants aged from 25 to 74 (avg. 49.7)
and described their visual impairment as blind (N=6) or having low
vision (N=3). Most participants had prior experiences using remote
sighted assistance (e.g., Be My Eyes [3], Aira [2]) and AI-enabled
services (e.g., Seeing AI [5], Be My AI [1]).
6.2
Procedure, Tasks and Analysis
The study consisted of three sessions: (i) a onboarding session, where
participants learned to use StateScribe; (ii) a main task session,
where participants were asked to identify changes in three different
scenarios, including a shared office, a grocery store, and an outdoor
courtyard; and (iii) an interview session, where participants reflected
on their experiences and responded to Likert-scale questions.
For each scenario in the main task session, participants first ex-
plored the environment and then revisited it. During each visit,
researchers introduced within-visit changes by moving objects in
real time to simulate common dynamics in shared or public spaces
(e.g., placing or removing items; Table 3). Examples included plac-
ing a bottle on a shared table, taking items in the grocery store, or
removing outdoor obstacles by workers (Table 3). Between visits,
the researcher introduced cross-visit changes to simulate longer-
term rearrangements (e.g., days or weeks). These included moving
chairs in the shared office, price changes in the grocery store, and
removing signage in the outdoor walkway. These changes approxi-
mated everyday dynamics within the time constraint of a two-hour
study. In total, the shared office and grocery store scenarios each
included 13 changes (8 within-visit, 5 cross-visit), while the outdoor
scenario included 12 changes (8 within-visit, 4 cross-visit).
During the study, participants independently explored the indoor
environments (e.g., a shared office and grocery store). In the outdoor
scenario, a researcher accompanied participants for safety, while
the participants retained full control over their exploration. In total,
we collected 18 visit records for the shared office (117 tasks = 9
participants × 13 changes), 16 for the grocery store (104 tasks = 8
participants × 13 changes; P9 excluded due to corrupted data), and

6.3.1
How effectively does StateScribe support users in per-

within around 10 minutes, achieving completion rates of 82.9%

office scenario, issues were mainly due to camera aiming: some re-

the cart from the aisle had a lower completion rate (50%) than in

7
Discussion and Future Work
We discuss our lessons learned and design implications for extend-
ing StateScribe to broader use cases in the long term.
Device choices and interface constraints. Camera-based ATs
face persistent challenges, including object aiming [24, 38, 39, 45,
52, 58], content coverage [28], and social acceptability [7, 36, 50].
StateScribe currently relies on sensory inputs from a smartphone
(RGB-D images and camera poses) to construct spatial memory.
However, a depth camera requires an RGB camera with a stan-
dard FoV for alignment, limiting coverage and demanding more
precise aiming. This may explain higher performance outdoors
(89.6%) than in denser indoor settings (82.7% grocery, 82.9% office).
Some participants also raised usability concerns about continuous
handheld use. We envision that StateScribe can generalize to such
wearables with RGB-D input and camera pose tracking to offer
hands-free interaction [14], though privacy and social concerns
could remain [7]. Finally, StateScribe required manual selection of
prior visits. Future work could enable automatic relocalization (e.g.,
via GPS) to streamline revisits.
Detecting more types of changes with additional sensors.
As noted in Section 4.1, StateScribe focuses on object-level changes,
enabling effective real-time detection and across revisits. However,
at 1 FPS, it may miss fast or transient changes (e.g., moving cars,
flashing lights, or human activities). Although increasing frame rate
could help, it may introduce trade-offs in computation, storage, and
retrieval. An alternative is to augment StateScribe with additional
sensors. For instance, event cameras can capture high-frequency
motion and light changes asynchronously, while infrared cameras
can detect otherwise invisible changes such as temperature varia-
tions (e.g., heating or cooling objects). Integrating these modalities
could expand the range of detectable changes and improve robust-
ness by referencing different sensor outputs.
Integrating different information cursors to deliver the
right information timely. StateScribe uses the user’s 3D loca-
tion (from camera pose) as an information cursor, a mechanism
to indicate information of interest, to retrieve memory, and detect
changes across revisits. However, our study showed that user needs
extended beyond change detection and vary by context, and State-
Scribe does not always surface the most relevant information in
time. For example, participants often held items and sought visual
details (e.g., color or flavor) in grocery settings, or needed detailed
information (e.g., whether stairs go up or down) and signage texts in
outdoor settings. These needs could be better supported by prior sys-
tems that use different user activities as information cursors, such
as leveraging hand-object interactions as intent cues [38, 39, 44],
or using camera motion to obtain adaptive visual details [11]. To-
gether, these works shift visual assistance from reactive question
answering to proactive interaction. However, effectively integrating
multiple information cursors and delivering the right information
at the right time remains an open challenge. Future work should
explore how to model user context, select appropriate information
cursors, and map user intent to timely descriptions.
Towards a long-term assistive AI companion. To our best
knowledge, StateScribe is the first AI-driven live description system
with memory for change detection, outperforming both a VLM-
only Live model and an Offline video model (Section 5.3.1). It also
scales to extended use across three scenarios with low latency and
memory overhead (Section 5.3.3). However, challenges remain in
making it a reliable long-term assistive companion. Participants
expected StateScribe to account for their assistive context (e.g.,
using a white cane) or information preference to reduce redun-
dant information, and to provide richer contextual reminders when
revisiting locations, similar to a human companion (Section 6.3).
Furthermore, memory should extend beyond object-level changes
to capture semantic relationships and structured knowledge within
environments. For example, participants wondered if StateScribe’s
memory could extend beyond individual object changes to a more
holistic, global understanding (e.g., store layout, aisle-level orga-
nization). This could be enabled by integrating structured scene
memory as an additional layer [20, 31, 68], potentially augmented
by community-contributed data collected over time. Future work
could explore designing AI companions that better model human-
like guidance, adapt to users’ evolving contexts, and integrate more
global, structured representations of space for meaningful interac-
tions.

Prompt 1: Visual Change Detection System Prompt
System Prompt
You are a highly conservative visual change detector. Compare two images of the same scene.
Goal: report only real, substantive scene-content changes, with confidence for each reported change.
Safety priority:
• A false positive is 100x worse than a miss.
• {"changes": []} is fully correct and preferred whenever there is any real ambiguity.
• Never invent a change or a bbox just to satisfy the JSON format.
• If a change is not clearly real, substantive, and tightly localizable, omit it.
• Low confidence is only for likely-real but weak/subtle changes. It is not permission to speculate.
Never report these:
• Viewpoint, perspective, or parallax differences from camera motion.
• Lighting, shadow, reflection, glare, exposure, or background ambiance changes.
• Apparent text loss caused by glare/exposure.
• Objects that only shifted position or orientation without a real state/content change, except for clear location changes of
large furniture or fixtures.
• Slight object movement or small repositioning.
• Count-only changes. Ignore quantity differences rather than reporting them as scene changes.
• Humans. Ignore people entirely and never place a bbox on them.
Rules:
• Output object-level changes only.
• Pay extra attention to substantive changes involving large objects or furniture, such as carts, chairs, tables, or similar large
fixtures.
• If a large object or furniture clearly moved from one place to another, treat it as two object-level events: one disappear at the
old location and one appear at the new location.
• Return at most 3 changes. If more than 3 plausible changes exist, keep only the 3 most important and most certain ones.
• Every change must include confidence: low, med, or high.
